title: Your Blessing Has Been Taken Away — Dim Eyes, Goatskins, a Bitter Cry
blocks: Brothers and sisters, peace to you. In all of Genesis, the chapter where family life is at its most shameful is the one in front of us today.

Let me say one thing before we begin. The most frightening thing in a household is not that somebody has committed some great sin. The most frightening thing is four people who each believe they are in the right — and who between them pull the house down.

Chapter 27 is exactly that kind of chapter. Isaac plays favourites, and although he knows perfectly well that God said, "The elder will serve the younger," he still means to bless Esau. Rebekah has the word of God, and she uses a deception to bring the word of God about. Jacob lies to his blind father, and puts God's name inside the lie. Esau sold his birthright long ago, and now he comes back wanting the blessing.
Four people. Not one of them is a villain — and every one of them is in the wrong.
Let me put the answer up front. God's will has never needed our lies in order to be accomplished. What you seize you can have at once — and the bill for it takes a full twenty years to pay off.
Verse 1: "When Isaac was old, and his eyes were dim, so that he could not see …"
Brothers and sisters, that sentence is the situation of the whole chapter: a man who cannot see has to tell two sons apart.
And whom does he call in? "He called Esau his elder son." הַגָּדֹל (*hagadol*) — the elder.
Put that line beside Genesis 25:23: "The elder will serve the younger." That is what God said with his own mouth to Rebekah. And Isaac calls in the elder — of all his sons, the elder.
Verse 4, he says: "Make me savory food, such as I love, and bring it to me, that I may eat, and that my soul may bless you before I die."
That word "savory food", מַטְעַמִּים (*mat'amim*), occurs six times in this chapter. The whole business turns on one meal.

Brothers and sisters, this is worth stopping over. A patriarch is about to hand on the covenant made with Abraham, and the way he sets the thing in motion is by ordering a dish. Genesis 25:28 says, "Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison" — his favouritism has a reason, and the reason is concrete, and physical, and it lives in his stomach.
Appetite never announces itself out loud. It simply tilts your judgement a little, quietly. It was not that Isaac did not know what God had said. It was that he wanted that venison more.
And verse 5: "Rebekah heard when Isaac spoke to Esau his son." The Hebrew uses a participle — she had been listening all along.

Brothers and sisters, that one line gives away the state of this household: the husband is talking to the elder son, and the wife is outside the door listening. Not one person in this family is open with anybody.
And when Rebekah passes the message on, she adds a line that Isaac never said. Verse 7: "Bring me venison, and make me savory food, that I may eat, and bless you before Yahweh before my death."
"Before Yahweh" — Isaac did not say that. She put it in.
Brothers and sisters, we have to be very careful here. Putting God's name into something we already wanted to do is the easiest form of manipulation there is.
All four people in this chapter are calculating. Why did God still let Jacob have the blessing?

Two things have to be kept apart: God's plan, and human method. God had already said back in chapter 25, "The elder will serve the younger" — the outcome was always going to be that. But in this chapter not one person acts according to what God said. Isaac insists on blessing Esau; Esau, who knows perfectly well that he sold the birthright, goes to collect the blessing anyway; Rebekah sets the trap; Jacob lies. God's plan came about, and all four of them paid for it: Rebekah never saw her son again, Jacob ran for twenty years, Esau spent half a lifetime hating, and Isaac was deceived and stayed deceived to the end of his days. So this chapter is not teaching us that a right outcome settles everything. It is showing us this: God is able to accomplish what he has purposed, and that does not mean we are excused from answering for the methods we used.
Isaac knew that God had said, "The elder will serve the younger." Why did he still want to bless Esau?

The clue the text gives is Genesis 25:28: "Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison." And what he asks for in 27:4 is "savory food, such as I love." So his favouritism has a taste to it and a stomach behind it. This is worth every parent's and every leader's while to think over: when we are especially indulgent towards one particular person, the reason is very often not a spiritual judgement at all — it is that he makes us comfortable. And here is the more serious thing. Isaac acted on his own preference while knowing exactly what God had said. That is what this lesson puts to us: favouritism plus authority will let a man go around even the word that God has spoken.
2. A Light from the Original: He Put God's Name Inside the Lie

In verses 11 to 13, Jacob's first reaction is not "this is wrong" but "this will get us caught": "Behold, Esau my brother is a hairy man, and I am a smooth man. What if my father touches me? I will seem to him as a deceiver, and I would bring a curse on myself, and not a blessing."
And Rebekah answers, "Let your curse be on me, my son. Only obey my voice …"

Brothers and sisters, she has already reckoned on the curse, and she goes ahead anyway. That is not faith. That is taking over. She remembers God's promise, and she does not believe God has any way of bringing it about himself.
And then comes the performance. Verse 18: Jacob goes in and says, "My father?" Isaac asks, "Who are you, my son?"
Jacob says, "I am Esau your firstborn."
Verse 20, Isaac asks, "How is it that you have found it so quickly, my son?"
And Jacob's answer is the heaviest sentence in the chapter:
"Because Yahweh your God gave me success."
Brothers and sisters, he has put God's name inside the lie.
And notice how he says it: "Yahweh your God." Not "my God" — "your God."
At this moment, for Jacob, Yahweh is still his father's God and not his own. Not until Bethel, in chapter 28, will he say it for himself: "Yahweh will be my God."
In verses 21 and 22 Isaac grows suspicious: "Please come near, that I may feel you, my son, whether you are really my son Esau or not." And then comes the famous line:
"The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau."

Brothers and sisters, every person who serves ought to keep that sentence by him. How often is it that our words are spiritual and our methods belong to the world? The voice is right; the hands are wrong.

In verse 27 Isaac feels him, smells him, and then blesses him. And look at what the blessing contains: "God give you of the dew of the sky, of the fatness of the earth, and plenty of grain and new wine. … Cursed be everyone who curses you. Blessed be everyone who blesses you." That last line is exactly what God said to Abraham in Genesis 12:3. The covenant made with Abraham passed into Jacob's hands over a plate of counterfeit venison.
Jacob said, "Because Yahweh your God gave me success." Why is that sentence especially terrible?

Because it is God's name put inside a lie. He has already said, "I am Esau your firstborn"; this next sentence goes one step further and uses God to underwrite his own falsehood. The Ten Commandments say, "You shall not misuse the name of Yahweh your God, for Yahweh will not hold him guiltless who misuses his name" — and this verse is a living example of it. That is a serious warning for us today. The most dangerous lie is not the barefaced one. It is the one with "this is God's leading" or "the Lord laid it on my heart" attached — because the other person has no way to argue back. And the practical boundary is clear enough: do not put God's name on something you are not sure of. Using God's name to push through the outcome you happen to want is taking the holiest thing there is and using it as a tool.
Isaac said, "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau." Why did he go ahead and bless him?

The text records his doubts the whole way along. He asks, "How is it that you have found it so quickly?" He calls him near so that he can feel him. He asks again, "Are you really my son Esau?" He even smells his clothing. Four checks, and every one of them turned up something that did not fit — and at the end of it he blessed him. What most interpreters observe is this: the answer he wanted in his heart outweighed the evidence in his hands. And that is intensely practical for us — a person is not really deceived by somebody else; he is deceived by the thing he himself wants. So when you are weighing something up, the moment to be most on your guard is the moment when you think, "This happens to be exactly what I wanted." In practice: when that moment comes, deliberately write down every point that does not fit, and find one person who will not simply agree with you, and have him look it over.
3. He Lifted Up His Voice and Wept
Verse 30: Jacob had only just gone out when Esau came in from his hunting.
Verse 33: "Isaac trembled violently, and said, 'Who, then, is he who has taken venison, and brought it to me, and I have eaten of all before you came, and have blessed him? Yes, he will be blessed.'"
Brothers and sisters, "trembled violently" — the Hebrew here is extremely strong. It is the kind of shock that sets a man's whole body shaking.
And notice the last thing he says: "Yes, he will be blessed."

He could perfectly well have said, "That does not count; I shall bless again." He did not. In that moment he understood one thing — this was not his to decide. All his life he had wanted to get around what God had said, and in the very moment he was deceived he suddenly saw the hand of God.
That line — "Yes, he will be blessed" — is the finest sentence this old man ever spoke. He surrendered.
Then verse 34: "When Esau heard the words of his father, he cried with an exceedingly great and bitter cry, and said to his father, 'Bless me, even me also, my father.'"
And verse 38: "Esau said to his father, 'Do you have just one blessing, my father? Bless me, even me also, my father.' Esau lifted up his voice, and wept."
Brothers and sisters — a hunter in the prime of his strength, weeping out loud in front of his father.
Hebrews 12:17 says, "For you know that even when he afterward desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no place for a change of mind though he sought it diligently with tears."

And notice what it is that he could not find — a place where a mind might be changed, so that a blessing already spoken could be called back. The verse is not saying that God refused him repentance. It is saying that the blessing had already gone out of the old man's mouth, and it could not be recalled.

And in verses 39 and 40, the words Isaac gives him can be rendered from the Hebrew as "your dwelling will be away from the fatness of the earth" — the little preposition מִן can mean "away from" quite as easily as "of". That is not a blessing; it is a forecast. But he does leave him one line at the end: "It will happen, when you will break loose, that you will shake his yoke from off your neck."
Verse 41: "Esau hated Jacob because of the blessing … Esau said in his heart, 'The days of mourning for my father are at hand. Then I will kill my brother Jacob.'"
And in verse 45 Rebekah says, "until your brother's anger turns away from you … Then I will send, and get you from there."

Brothers and sisters, this is the heaviest sentence in the chapter. She said "a few days" — stay with him a few days. It turned out to be twenty years. And Scripture never once records that she saw Jacob again. The mother never again laid eyes on the son she loved most.
Esau cried "with an exceedingly great and bitter cry", and yet Hebrews says he found no place for a change of mind. Is that not a contradiction?

Hebrews 12:17 says, "For you know that even when he afterward desired to inherit the blessing, he was rejected, for he found no place for a change of mind though he sought it diligently with tears." Notice what that change of mind is about — it is about getting the blessing back, about a mind in his father that might yet be turned. It is not about God refusing to pardon him. Which is to say: what he wept over was the outcome he had lost. Nowhere does Scripture say that he repented of the attitude that sold the birthright in the first place. And that gives us a distinction that goes straight to the bone: being sorry about a consequence and repenting of the thing itself are two different matters. Everybody can manage the first; only the second changes a person. And the way to tell them apart is to ask yourself this: if that thing had not turned out badly, would I still think it was wrong?
Brothers and sisters, I want you to look at the receipt for all this.
Jacob got the blessing — that part is genuine, and God never took it back. But here is what came next.
He had to run that same night, and he was away from home for twenty years.

Chapter 29: he loves Rachel, he works seven years, and on the morning after the wedding he lifts the veil — and it is Leah. He had deceived his father by passing himself off as the firstborn son; now he is swindled with a firstborn daughter. And Laban's reason is this: "It is not done so in our place, to give the younger before the firstborn."
Chapter 31: he says that Laban changed his wages ten times over.
Chapter 37: his own sons bring him a bloodstained coat to deceive him with — he had deceived his blind father with the skins of young goats, and now he is deceived with the blood of a goat.
Brothers and sisters, Galatians 6:7 says, "Don't be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap."
And let me say it very plainly: God's will was accomplished, and not one penny came off the bill.

So "God will work all things together for good anyway" is not a reason to put out your hand. God will indeed clear the mess up — and you are the one who has to walk through the clearing up. What this chapter teaches is not that God will tidy up after you. It is that some school fees never needed paying at all.
Rebekah said, "Let your curse be on me, my son." Was that not a brave sort of mother's love?

She did carry it, yes — and this chapter does not hold her up as a role model. Look at what her method produced. She told her son to run and stay away a few days; in fact it was twenty years, and Scripture never again records that she saw Jacob. Not even her death is recorded; the one later mention comes in chapter 49, where we are told she was buried in the cave of Machpelah. So the price of that sentence — she paid it herself. And that is a deep warning to parents: shouldering the consequences for your child sounds magnificent, but if you are doing it in order to bring about the outcome that you yourself want, that shouldering will turn into a lifetime of loss. Real protection is not taking the child into the scheme in the first place.
5. Distortions You Must Be Able to Spot

The first is preaching Jacob's deception as the initiative of a man with faith. Some will say that he "had a real hunger for spiritual blessing." But the twenty years that follow are the bill for this business, and Scripture nowhere underwrites his methods. Dress him up and what your congregation learns from you is the art of spiritual packaging.

The second is saying that because God permitted it, God approved of it. Permitting and approving are two different things. Lot, David and Jacob were all disciplined under one and the same principle. Blur the two together and your congregation goes numb about sin.

The third is making Rebekah the one villain of the chapter. Isaac knew what God had said and set out to bless Esau anyway; Jacob went along with the scheme of his own accord and lied using God's name; Esau had long since despised his birthright. Blame one person only, and your congregation will go looking for the answer in somebody else.

The fourth is using Esau's weeping to frighten people with "you may leave repentance too late." What Hebrews is talking about is the content of his remorse — what he wanted was the inheritance, not a heart turned back to God. Preach it as God turning away a man who repents, and you will drive to despair the very people who genuinely want to repent. Peter denied the Lord too, and after he wept he was restored.

The fifth is skipping over Isaac's line, "Yes, he will be blessed." That is the turning point of the whole chapter — an old man who had spent his life trying to get around the word of God surrendered in the very moment he was deceived. Preach only his favouritism, and your congregation never sees how God works at the far end of a person's life.
6. Two Real Questions from a Chinese Setting

The first question: the commonest wound in a Chinese family is favouritism — sons valued above daughters, the child who does well at school preferred, the obedient one preferred. What does this chapter say about that? Brothers and sisters, the answer this chapter gives is not a maxim; it is an ending. Nobody in that household wins. The father is deceived, the mother loses the son she loves most, and the two brothers are separated for twenty years. And the starting point of that ending is one perfectly ordinary sentence in Genesis 25:28: "Now Isaac loved Esau, because he ate his venison. Rebekah loved Jacob." Favouritism is not built in a day. It starts with "he is the more affectionate one", "he is more like me." And let me say something very practical to the parents in the room: the children know. You think you have hidden it well; in fact the child who is not the favoured one has known since he was very small. If there is a child in your house who knows that he is not the one, then this chapter is the alarm bell ringing for you.

The second question: I have seen something in church that was achieved by dishonest means, and yet the result looks very good — the giving went up, the numbers went up, the ministry came off. How am I to think about that? Brothers and sisters, this chapter gives the most direct answer there is: Jacob got the blessing, and God did not take it back — and the bill came. So let me ask you to keep three things clear. First, a good result does not mean a right process. In 1 Samuel 15 Saul kept back the best of the sheep and the cattle to sacrifice to God, and Samuel said, "Behold, to obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams." Second, the bill usually does not arrive straight away. Jacob's arrived in instalments — seven years later, twenty years later, thirty years later. So "nothing has gone wrong so far" is not evidence of anything. Third, and this is the most practical of all: what you can do is keep your own hands clean. You may not be able to stop anybody else, but you can decide that you will not use that method yourself. And Isaac's last word — "Yes, he will be blessed" — reminds us of this: God's plan does not hang on our manoeuvring, and so we can afford to be honest.
Favouritism has already cracked my family open. Is there any saving it?

There is, but it has to be done in order. First, admit it. The most wounding thing about favouritism is not the behaviour; it is that everybody knows and nobody says it. If the older generation can manage one sentence — "I know that I was partial, back then" — that one sentence carries more power than ten years of making it up to somebody. Second, be specific. Do not merely say, "I treated you all the same." Name one thing: what I gave to whom in that particular year, the time I did not speak up for you. Third, time. The one who was passed over needs time; do not ask him to forgive on the spot. Fourth, if the relationship has been broken off for years, begin with one short message, and do not expect a single meeting to settle the whole thing.
7. Living 321 Out — Not Letting Preference Decide Spiritual Things
Brothers and sisters, let us bring this lesson back to the Three Foundations, the Two Core Values and the Goal of 321.

Jesus is my role model — Jacob went after the blessing under another man's name, wearing his brother's clothes with the skins of goats fastened over his own. And Philippians 2 says of the Lord Jesus that he, "existing in the form of God, didn't consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant." Brothers and sisters, one man took a name that was not his in order to get; the Other laid down what was his in order to give. My role model is this: he had no need to snatch — he chose to give himself away.

The Bible is my standard — Isaac knew what God had said; Genesis 25:23 stands there in the text. And he called in the elder son all the same. So the trouble with a standard is very often not whether you know it. It is whether you are willing to let it beat your own preference.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — from beginning to end of this chapter, not one person inquires of God. Four people, four sets of calculations, and not one of them kneels down to ask a single question. And in the very next chapter God appears unasked, on the first night of Jacob's flight. Brothers and sisters, God had not left this family. It was that nobody in this family opened his mouth.

Let Jesus be King — Isaac knew the word of God, and blessed according to his own palate. Appetite tilts judgement, and it does it quietly. To let Jesus be King is to stop letting your own preferences decide spiritual things: the person I like is not therefore the person God intends to use, and the style I find easy to swallow is not therefore the right one.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — there is an embarrassing fact in this chapter. God's plan was accomplished, and the glory rests on none of the four of them. Not one of them comes out of it with any dignity, and the promise goes on its way regardless. So we have nothing whatever to boast of — even the thing we are holding in our hands did not come to us because we won it handsomely.

Establish God's system — the covenant made with Abraham passed into Jacob's hands over a plate of counterfeit venison. Brothers and sisters, on one side that is a comfort: God's plan is not thrown off course by human sin, and the system does not hang on human perfection. On the other side it is a warning: that the plan was not thrown off course does not mean nobody pays.

And here I want to say something honest about 321 itself. We put a great deal of weight on calling, on vision, on doing great things for God. And this chapter is a very serious reminder to us. Everything Rebekah did, she did in order to bring about what God had said. Her aim was entirely correct. And she used her own methods to accomplish God's purpose, and the cost of it was the whole family. So fix this sentence in your memory: the goal is God's and the method is mine — that is not obedience, that is unbelief. Any piece of work that needs a little deception, a little manoeuvring, a little withholding of the truth for people's own good in order to move forward, has to be stopped and asked about all over again.
8. Four Kinds of Heart, One Question: "Who Are You?"
Brothers and sisters, Isaac asked one question: "Who are you, my son?" That sentence, falling into four different hearts, sounds like four completely different things.

The proud heart says, "What a dreadful family." This heart finishes the chapter busy ranking the four of them, working out which was worst. Brothers and sisters, notice this: the chapter passes not one word of comment. The author simply sets the events down and lets the twenty-year bill that follows do the talking. And the better question is this one: of these four, which am I most like?

The fearful heart says, "Then the things I have — is there a bill on those as well?" This heart starts turning over its own past. To a heart like that I want to say: if there really is something you obtained by the wrong means, then the right way to deal with it is not panic. It is admitting and returning — return what can be returned, own what cannot. Zacchaeus said, "If I have wrongfully exacted anything of anyone, I restore four times as much," and the Lord Jesus said, "Today, salvation has come to this house."

The ashamed heart says, "I am the one who was never the favourite." It may be that all your life you have known you were not the one in your family. Brothers and sisters, there is a fact in this chapter that is very easily missed: the son the father favoured is the one who ended up losing the blessing, and the son the father did not favour is the one God chose. Your parents' preference does not decide God's choosing.

The wounded heart says, "I am Esau, the one crying out loud." It may be that something really was taken from you — a position, the credit for a piece of work, a relationship — and that the one who took it is doing perfectly well on it. Brothers and sisters, let me point out three things. First, Scripture records his weeping in full; it never once tells him to be strong. Second, God gave him Mount Seir and made him into a nation — he was not thrown away. Third, in chapter 33 he runs towards the very brother who cheated him, throws his arms round him and kisses him, and the two of them weep. Of the work God did in that man Scripture writes not a single word — and that embrace was real. God is doing that same unwritten work in you.
9. This Week, a Few Things You Can Do

First, check your own "savory food." Is there one very concrete preference of yours — a type of person, a style of thing, something that makes you comfortable — that is quietly bending your spiritual judgement? Write it down.

Second, find one instance of "right voice, wrong hands." Was there something this week where what you said was thoroughly spiritual and what you did was not altogether clean? Leave other people's for now. Deal with that one of your own first.

Third, do not borrow God's name inside your sentences. This week, watch yourself when you say "God led me" or "God told me", and ask whether you are underwriting something you already wanted to do. Change it to this: "Here is what I think after praying about it … have a look at it with me."

Fourth, say something to one person you have been partial about. If you are a parent, a manager or a small-group leader, think about who "the one who is not the favourite" is, and go and find him this week and say a few words to him.

Fifth, this week tell this lesson to one friend outside the church, in three sentences: there is a household of four in the Bible — a father who played favourites, a mother who set the trap, a younger son who took his brother's name, and an elder son who had sold his birthright long before, and all four of them thought they were in the right; the man who cheated his way to the blessing then spent twenty years on the run, and was cheated several times over by exactly the same method; so here is the thing I learned — even when the goal is right, if you get it by the wrong means, you are still the one who pays the bill.
Brothers and sisters, let us declare together before God:
I declare that I will not use my own methods to accomplish God's purposes; that is not obedience, it is unbelief.
I declare that I will not put God's name into something that I already wanted to do.
I declare that I will not let my own preferences decide my spiritual judgement.
I declare that God's plan does not hang on my manoeuvring, and so I can afford to be honest.
This week's exercise is to say one true sentence without God's name attached. How is that actually done?

Three checks that work well. First, take the "the Lord laid it on my heart" and "God led me" sentences you have said recently and look at them: which of them actually means "I want this"? Try putting each one back into its plain form and see how it reads. Second, when you are making a decision, explain the reasons to people first without God's name anywhere in them — if the reason will not stand on its own, adding God's name to it will not make it stand. Third, if you genuinely do believe that something is God's guidance, then say it like this: "This is my judgement after praying about it, and I may be wrong." That way of speaking is honest, and it leaves room for the thing to be tested. And you will find that people trust a person who is willing to talk like that a great deal more, not less.
Brothers and sisters, if only one sentence from this lesson may remain, let it be verse 22:
"The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau."
A blind old man, feeling his son's hands, listening to his son's voice, sensing that something somewhere is not right — and unable to tell what.
Brothers and sisters, that sentence is the heaviest warning this chapter gives the church.

How much among us is a matter of a very spiritual voice and very worldly hands? We speak with God's name and we work by the world's methods. Our sermons are impeccable and our administration is calculating. We are devout when we pray, and shrewd when the door is shut and the terms are being agreed.
What Isaac touched was skin, what he smelled was clothing, what he heard was a voice — three senses gave him three answers, and he chose to believe the one he would rather believe.
But the chapter does not stop there.
In verse 33 the old man trembles violently, and then says the finest sentence of his whole life: "Yes, he will be blessed."
All his life he had wanted to get around what God said, and in the moment he was deceived, he finally surrendered.

Brothers and sisters, God has ways of pulling a person back at the very last stage of his life. Isaac was blind, he was deceived, he had lost control of everything — and in that moment he said one thing right.

And the man who cheated his way to the blessing had twenty years of road in front of him, until that night at the ford of the Jabbok, when someone asked him, "What is your name?" and he finally told the truth: "Jacob."

The focus is not on what I managed to get hold of, not on who deceived whom, and not on how broken this family was. The focus is on Jesus — he had no need to snatch, he chose to give himself away; he took no name that was not his, and he carried our name for us. Not I, but Christ.
May God bless every one of us: this week, to look our own hands over once, and to say a few words to the one who has never been the favourite. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray, amen.

Leader's note: the Three Transformations are one road running downward. The first drives the point into the head; the second carries it from the head into the heart; the third carries it from the heart into the days of the week. If time runs short, cover fewer questions rather than skipping the third — without reaching the third transformation, this lesson stops at a mindset.

Priority markers: ★★★ = highest priority; if time is short, discuss at least this one in each transformation. ★★ = second priority. ★ = if time allows. The multiplication assignment marked [Must do] may not be dropped; it can be finished at home.
Transformation One | Internalise — until it becomes mindset (about 20 minutes)
Purpose: through discussion, to drive the point of this lesson into a clear mindset.
1. ★★★ God's plan came about, and all four of them still paid for it. How does that correct the idea that a right outcome settles everything?
2. ★★ Jacob put God's name inside a lie. What does that kind of talk look like today? Which version of it have you heard?
3. ★ Isaac checked four times and blessed him anyway. Are people deceived by somebody else, or by the thing they themselves want?
4. ★★ Esau wept bitterly, and never repented of having sold the birthright. What is the difference between being sorry about a consequence and repenting of the thing itself?
Leader's reminder: the aim of this section is that people can say it, not that they answer beautifully. If someone is speaking in fragments, help him tidy it up; do not finish his sentence for him.
Transformation Two | Digest — until it becomes life (about 35 minutes · the heart of this lesson)
Purpose: through seeing, listening, thinking, speaking and doing, to digest the mindset until it becomes life.

5. ★★★ The manuscript named four kinds of heart — proud (I will get this settled for God myself), fearful (if I do not grab it there will be nothing left), ashamed (I have used methods that were not clean), wounded (I am the one in the family who never got blessed). Which are you most like? What experience made you that way?
6. ★★ Read aloud: "The voice is Jacob's voice, but the hands are the hands of Esau." Then tell the group — where does that sentence touch you?
7. ★★ The last decision you made: was there a moment in it when you thought, "This happens to be exactly what I wanted"? Which point that did not fit did you ignore at the time?
8. ★ Finish this in one sentence: "In the family I grew up in, which of these four was I?"
9. ★★ This week, to whom will you say, "I know that I was partial, back then", or "I got that wrong"? Say the name, and say when.

Leader's reminder: this lesson will lift the lid on favouritism at home and on the wound of being the one passed over. The leader speaks about his own first. Do not let group members pass comment on one another's families, and do not require anyone to forgive on the spot. If anyone breaks down, stop and stay with him, and follow up with him privately after the meeting.
Transformation Three | Transform — until it becomes daily living (about 25 minutes)
Purpose: through discussing concrete application, to transform life into daily living.
10. ★★ In your own family, who is the "Esau" — the one who is still waiting for a word of blessing? What will you say to him this week?
11. ★ The same question in another setting: at work, or in your ministry, who is the one who keeps being passed over?

12. ★★★ The practice of leaving God's name out: this week, anything you were about to push forward with "God laid it on my heart", put instead as "this is my judgement, and I may be wrong." Say what the matter is that you are about to raise.
13. ★★ The 920 practice: find your one "2" — your spiritual companion — and ask him, this week, whenever you say "the Lord led me", to ask you back, "Is that what you wanted?" Say his name now.

14. ★★★ [Must do] Multiplication assignment: this week, tell this lesson to one friend outside the church in three sentences. First: there is a man in the Bible who cheated his brother out of his blessing, and said while he was doing it, "Yahweh your God gave me success." Second: he ended up on the run for twenty years, and his mother never saw him again. Third: so what I learned is that putting God's name onto the thing you yourself want is a terrible thing to do. Write down now who you are going to tell.

In pairs, tell each other two things: the sentence you are going to say to somebody this week, and the recent moment when you thought, "This happens to be exactly what I wanted." Then pray for each other, asking the Lord to keep us from using his name to underwrite the things we want.
